speaker: Noam Brown
title: Really Big Test-Time Compute in AI with OpenAI's Noam Brown
question: In frontier AI, why do standard single-number benchmark tables often misrepresent how much better a new reasoning model actually is?
guest: Whenever a new model is released, there's this benchmark grid with a single number for a model on a single benchmark. When we released 5.5, on paper it was only a few percentage points better than 5.4, so people were skeptical until they actually played around with it. The reason it doesn't show up as so much better is that benchmark results aren't controlling for the amount of test-time compute being used. It turned out 5.5 is just much more efficient with its thinking—at max settings, 5.4 thinks for a lot longer. Once you control for thinking time, 5.5 is a substantial jump. People usually ask, 'Why not just evaluate until performance plateaus?' Back in GPT-3 land, models couldn't think productively for long, so you could run them until they plateaued. Today, modern scaffolded models can think for weeks before performance plateaus, which is simply too far out to reasonably test. The proper way to evaluate models now is to set a budget—tokens, cost, or time—or plot performance as a function of test-time compute.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
A single score collapses several things that matter into one figure and hides the conditions under which it was produced.

First, reasoning models don't have one performance level: their accuracy depends on how much thinking budget, tool access, scaffolding and number of attempts they were given. A table rarely holds those constant, so a "win" may just reflect more compute spent per task, with cost and latency left out. The honest comparison is a cost-versus-performance curve, not a point.

Second, many headline benchmarks are saturated or contaminated. When top models score in the 90s, the remaining gap is mostly label noise and leaked test items, so real capability gains get compressed into a point or two, while memorisation can inflate others.

Third, percentages are nonlinear. Going from 90% to 95% halves the error rate, and small per-step reliability gains compound into large differences on long, multi-step tasks, which accuracy tables understate.

Finally, averages hide variance: run-to-run noise, small sample sizes, missing confidence intervals, selective reporting by vendors, and uneven gains across task difficulty mean a one-number difference can either overstate or understate the real improvement.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Standard single-number benchmark tables collapse a multi-dimensional trade-off into one static point, obscuring how a score was achieved. Because reasoning models trade test-time compute for accuracy—generating thousands of thinking tokens, sampling parallel rollouts, or applying majority voting—a higher score often reflects spending vastly more inference budget, latency, and money rather than advancing the true compute-accuracy Pareto frontier. Leaderboards also routinely mix incompatible evaluation setups, comparing single-try accuracy against consensus voting, custom agentic scaffolding, or maximum reasoning-effort budgets.

Moreover, headline benchmarks skew heavily toward narrow, automatically verifiable puzzles like competition math and self-contained coding—the exact distributions targeted during reinforcement learning. Tiny evaluation sets like AIME introduce high statistical noise, benchmark saturation compresses meaningful capability gaps, and subtle training contamination inflates reported gains. Consequently, a dramatic jump in a single table number can mask stagnant token efficiency and fail to predict reliability on messy, open-ended real-world tasks where clean verification signals do not exist.

noweb.answer:
Standard single-number benchmark tables reduce complex trade-offs to raw accuracy, hiding the test-time compute required to achieve a score. Frontier reasoning models often boost performance by generating tens of thousands of hidden chain-of-thought tokens, meaning a higher score may simply reflect spending orders of magnitude more money and latency rather than a genuine leap in underlying capability or efficiency. Comparing reasoning models fairly requires evaluating accuracy against inference cost along a Pareto frontier, yet static leaderboards omit this dimension entirely.

Single numbers also obscure mismatched evaluation protocols, such as comparing a baseline’s single-attempt accuracy against a new model’s score inflated by majority voting, repeated sampling, or custom tool scaffolding. Finally, static benchmarks suffer from ceiling effects, training data contamination, and narrow problem formats. Near saturation, tiny percentage differences can either compress major capability gaps or reflect grading noise, while steep gains on self-contained math and coding puzzles frequently fail to generalize to ambiguous, real-world workflows where consistency, instruction following, and calibration matter far more than peak puzzle-solving accuracy.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Single-number tables hide the conditions behind each score, and with reasoning models those conditions can matter as much as the model itself.

The biggest factor is test-time compute. A reasoning model's accuracy rises with how many tokens it is allowed to "think," and also with whether results are reported as one attempt or as the best or majority answer over many samples. So "85% vs. 78%" may compare a model running a huge thinking budget with parallel sampling against a rival limited to one short pass. Cost and latency, which can differ by ten times or more, usually don't appear at all.

Scaffolding is not standardized either. Tool access, custom prompts, agent harnesses and retry rules shift scores a lot, especially on coding and agentic benchmarks.

Small benchmarks are statistically noisy. AIME has 30 problems, so one question is worth about 3 points, and run-to-run variance can be as large as the claimed gain. Results are rarely shown with confidence intervals.

Finally, many benchmarks are saturated or contaminated. When the training data likely included the test items, or scores sit near the ceiling, the gaps show memorization and leftover noise rather than better reasoning. Labs also choose which favorable results to report.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Standard single-number benchmark tables collapse a complex performance profile into one headline score, hiding the trade-offs that matter most for reasoning models. First, they obscure inference-time compute: a model may post a higher score simply by spending far more thinking tokens, latency, and cost, or by relying on test-time scaffolds like majority voting and tool access, rather than being fundamentally more capable per unit of compute. Second, many flagship benchmarks are saturated or small, so genuine capability leaps compress into tiny percentage gains while run-to-run variance and labeling noise masquerade as real progress. Third, public test sets suffer from data contamination and targeted reinforcement learning, allowing models to overfit narrow, easily verifiable puzzles without generalizing to messy, open-ended real-world work. Finally, aggregate averages mask reliability, since two models with identical pass rates can differ sharply in calibration, consistency, and failure severity. Without reporting cost-performance curves, evaluation harnesses, and variance, a single score makes apples-to-apples comparisons deeply misleading.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A benchmark score averages over a fixed set of tasks, so it can hide where a reasoning model improved. If most questions are already easy for both models, a breakthrough on the hardest problems may move the average only a few points. Conversely, a large gain on a narrow benchmark may barely matter for the work you care about.

The score also hides what it took to get there. A model given more time to reason, access to tools, or several attempts can outperform one answering in a single try. And two models with the same average can behave very differently in a workflow where every step has to succeed.

To judge the improvement, look at which problems the model can now solve, how consistently it solves them, and what it costs in time and compute under comparable conditions.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A benchmark score is an average over a particular set of questions under particular test conditions. An increase from 95% to 97% looks small, yet it cuts the error rate by 40%. Whether that matters in practice depends on which errors disappeared. A model might solve a class of hard problems its predecessor consistently missed, or gain the same two points on routine questions while still failing on the problems you care about.

For reasoning models, the score also depends on how much time and compute the model gets. Multiple attempts or tool access can improve accuracy, so a higher score alone doesn’t tell you whether the new model is more accurate at the same cost. Small gaps can also fall within statistical uncertainty. The clearest comparisons show where the gains occur and how accuracy changes as the time or compute budget increases.
